articles.title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
articles.summary: The most revealing thing about the summit in Washington may be what the two leaders did not say - and what we still don't know.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Xi and Trump's talks in Washington yielded no joint statements and few major breakthroughs By Laura Bicker China correspondent 
- Published 28 September 2026 
On Monday, China released more information of what was agreed at the talks between Xi Jinping and Donald Tump last week, shedding light on a handful of concrete outcomes. 
But there were no joint statements and few major breakthroughs. 
Instead, both governments issued separate accounts of the meeting - perhaps a sign that despite the White House tours and promise of warmer ties, Washington and Beijing remain wary of each other. 
Here are four things we now know - and still don't - about what transpired at the talks. 
A new AI dialogue and communication channel 
Beijing says it has agreed with Washington to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for the end of November. 
As both countries race to develop advanced artificial intelligence, the move suggests they see a need for some guardrails around a technology that is increasingly being used in everything from business to military planning. 
They have also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents, aimed at preventing misunderstandings or unexpected developments from turning into a broader confrontation. 
The meeting was being closely watched for any developments or agreements in relation to AI - especially in the wake of calls by US companies like Anthropic to slow down developments, and revelations that Open AI had gained unauthorised access to government websites in countries like Australia and had "meddled" with multiple US government agency sites.

- Published 5 days ago 
Trade truce - what was included and what was left out 
Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January. 
The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year. 
Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December. 
It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently. 
But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough. 
China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing. 
Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs. 
The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028. 
What is striking is what was left out. 
There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Chinese toys heading to American stores will benefit from the lower tariffs 
The US left out Taiwan - but China didn't 
The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping. 
According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution. 
After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack. 
He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue. 
This time, Trump disclosed far less. 
"We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend. 
"Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel." 
That silence may be significant. 
Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months. 
Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit. 
The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so. 
Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. 
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, 
The issue of Taiwan was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping 
China may be opening the investment doors 
China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations. 
The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it. 
Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed. 
Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen. 
And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans. 
Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention. 
So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place. 
So what do we know? 
This summit produced more dialogue - but very little decision change for now. The most contentious issues from advanced technology to Taiwan remain unresolved. 
But for both leaders, this is a familiar outcome - a promise of more channels of communication, modest economic concessions and modest proposals to steady relations. 
And while both remain committed to a steady relationship - continued US-China dialogue appears far easier than asking either superpower to compromise.

articles.title: Trump and Xi exchange warm words at state dinner but little progress on key issues
articles.summary: Despite diplomatic niceties and gifts, little was shared on substantial issues separating the leaders.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? By Bernd Debusmann ,  White House reporter ,  Max Matza   and   Ione Wells ,  Reporting from Washington 
- Published 25 September 2026 
US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping exchanged warm words at a lavish White House state dinner but gave little indication of progress on pressing issues. 
Xi stressed that they should ensure AI remain "under human control" and act "as responsible major countries", while Trump toasted a future of "harmony, peace and success" for both nations. 
But tensions remain despite the diplomatic niceties, including over Taiwan - with Xi urging Trump earlier in the day to take the "correct position" on the self-governing island which Beijing claims, amid a weapons package paused by Trump. 
Billionaire business leaders and US tech CEOs joined the leaders at the extravagant dinner late on Thursday. 
Their arrival was marked by protesters shouting from just outside the White House gates, some of whom were arrested. 
Trump lavished praise on Xi during his first visit to the US in over a decade, telling those attending the dinner that while the two countries had "different systems", they had "never gotten along better". 
Xi meanwhile welcomed the "historic juncture" in US-China relations - and said both leaders' ambitions could "surely be mutually reinforcing". 
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries to meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times, and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said. 
While Xi said he and Trump had shared "in-depth exchanges and reached common understanding on many issues", little mention was made of the crucial matters which divide the leaders of the world's two most powerful countries. 
China believes the US is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan. 
Trump has meanwhile been expected to aim for deals around trade and tariffs during the visit – like lowering Chinese tariffs on American goods, increasing imports of Chinese rare earth minerals, and increasing exports of US agricultural products. 
Back at the White House after the dinner on Friday morning, Xi said he believed he and Trump were "charting the course for the great shift of China-US relations". 
He also confirmed that the two men would meet two more times by year's end, at the end of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or Apec, leaders' meeting in Shenzhen, China in November and again at the G20 held in Florida in November. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration" 
Trump has been blunt about his ambitions for artificial intelligence (AI) - and clear that he considers China to be the US's main rival for its development. 
But beyond Xi's reference to AI remaining under "human control", little indication was given of what progress the two leaders may have made on the issue during their talks. 
The dinner also came just hours after Chinese state media reported Xi had, behind closed doors, advised Washington to handle "with prudence" its approach to Taiwan. Washington is yet to comment publicly on the remarks. 
The US is legally bound to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but Trump delayed approving a $14bn (£11bn) arms package for it after Xi in May warned that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict". 
At the time, Trump called it a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.

- Published 5 days ago

- Published 3 days ago 
The evening marked a continuation of the lavish welcome Xi has so far received in the US. 
Trump presented the Chinese president with a sculpture of a bald eagle - America's national symbol - saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America". First Lady Melania had participated in its design, Trump added. 
Others in attendance included key White House figures, such as Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, chief of staff Monica Crowley, and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. 
They were joined by scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and corporate executives. 
Apple's Tim Cook and Nvidia's Jensen Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi, as was Elon Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government. 
OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, and Amazon's Jeff Bezos were also present, as were Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Yass, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Musk was seen mingling with guests, alongside US Secretary of State Marco Rubio 
The leaders of companies including General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance and ExxonMobil could also be seen in the room. 
"Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more." 
One notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Business leaders and tech bosses were among those in attendance 
The office of the First Lady Melania Trump, which planned the event, said the dinner menu would showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence". 
The first course was yellow squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta. The guests ate off red tablecloths - red being a symbol of luck and good fortune in China. 
For their main course they dined on a sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and roasted eggplant. 
Dessert featured the two leaders and their fellow diners tucking into vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit, with an accompanying ice cream "made with harvested White House honey". 
The wine chosen by the first lady included Schramsberg Blanc De Noir - a nod to President Nixon's 1972 "Toast to Peace" with former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, when they used a bottle from the same vineyard. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Trump puts on a warm reception for Xi in Washington 
Trump and Xi began the final day of their visit on Friday with tea at the White House's Red Room with their wives. 
The group then headed to the US National Archives for a tour of the building and its exhibits. 
Formally called the National Archives and Records Administration, the building holds some of the most important documents regarding the founding of the United States - including the US Constitution, the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights. 
Xi and his wife are expected to depart Washington later in the day.

articles.title: Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
articles.summary: China wanted progress on trade, technology and Taiwan - but hasn't got as much as it would have hoped for.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? By Laura Bicker China correspondent 
- Published 25 September 2026 
President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim. 
China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan. 
On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted. 
The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January. 
Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency. 
This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations. 
This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House 
The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes. 
Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year. 
On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China. 
The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself. 
In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict". 
Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing. 
Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict. 
On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence. 
However, Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Trade is helping to prop up growth 
The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards. 
All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans. 
But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax". 
And, of course, let's not forget the pandas . The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes. 
There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures 
But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics. 
The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal. 
Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive. 
Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower. 
The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever.

articles.title: Why Trump gave Xi an ornate bald eagle statue at the state dinner
articles.summary: From redwood benches to DVDs, gifts are an important part of the art of diplomacy.
articles.full_text:
Image source, EPA Image caption, 
President Trump said he and First Lady Melania helped design the statue By Brandon Drenon and Sareen Habeshian 
- Published 25 September 2026 
US President Donald Trump has presented Chinese President Xi Jinping with a sculpture of a bald eagle, a bird native to North America and his country's national symbol, during a lavish state dinner in Washington. 
The gift, which was unveiled before VIP guests at the Thursday dinner, embodies "the free and soaring spirit of America", said Trump . 
He said that he and First Lady Melania Trump participated in its design. The statue is part of a valuable - but sometimes tricky - aspect of international diplomacy: gift-giving. 
Such gifts are a small but meaningful element of the larger aim of Xi and Trump's three-day summit – forging personal relationships between heads of two global superpowers. 
Image source, EPA 
"They're going to discuss all of these complicated issues," Daniel Kritenbrink, partner at The Asia Group says. "But at the end of the day, these are still two human beings. 
"So that personal relationship means something," he says. "I think the gift exchange is one key part of that." 
Kritenbrink, who spent over 30 years as a US diplomat, mostly in Asia, says personal relationships are of particular importance to Xi. 
He believes the direct Trump-Xi bond is the glue that is holding together "the most complex and the most consequential relationship in the world". 
He says Trump, too, values what Kritenbrink calls "leader-level diplomacy". 
Gifts have had a unique presence in the Trump presidency. 
The US president has received a luxury jumbo jet, an engraved gold bar, a diamond-and-jewel encrusted gold ring, and more. 
Ole Jacob Sending from the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs says: "You think about the Trump presidency in that way, I think gift giving, certainly broadly defined, is very much part of how he operates." 
On Thursday morning, Xi announced a gift of two Chinese pandas to a zoo in Atlanta - and a new student exchange programme, which will welcome 100,000 US students to study in China over five years. 
"The giant panda have been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and the Americans," Xi said. "In a few days, two pandas - Ping Ping and Fu Shuang - will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people." 
It's unclear if he gave any further presents. The BBC has contacted the White House. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? 
Today, the practice of giving lavish gifts mostly exists in Gulf states and autocratic governments. 
"Autocracies like China give much more expensive gifts," says Morten Skumsrud Andersen, who co-authored a study on diplomacy and gifts with Sending. 
In the West, Andersen says, the tradition has been watered down by democratic guardrails and restrictions. 
For example, the US Constitution has an emoluments clause that puts a dollar-value limit on gifts a president can receive from a foreign government. 
Currently, the limit is $525 (£397). Anything higher and it becomes federal property, unless the president chooses to buy it back with his own money. 
Also, when giving a gift beyond a certain amount, a US president would have to go through Congress, unless he was paying for it personally. 
"There are a lot of rules and protocols involved," Sending says, "A lot of thought and process relating to what type of gift to to give, where should the gift exchange happen? How should it happen? When? 
"All of this is highly scripted, and involves negotiation at lower levels that goes on for weeks and weeks in advance," Sending says. 
Anderson adds: "This is not a last-minute purchase at the airport." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The bald eagle has become an American icon 
During Xi's state visit to the US in 2013, then-President Barack Obama gifted him an inscribed bench made of redwood, native to California where the two had met. They sat on it together afterwards, smiling for cameras. 
It was a more shining example than in 2009, when then-British Prime Minister Gordon Brown gifted Obama an ornamental desk pen holder made from the timbers of a historic anti-slave ship; while Obama gave Brown a set of DVDs, which reportedly were not formatted for UK DVD players. 
"That's one example of a kind of an embarrassing exchange," Sending says. 
Fortunately, Brown and Obama were allied leaders and not deep rivals looking to resolve seemingly intractable differences. 
"You don't want to mess up," Sending says, adding that the wrong gift could potentially derail any larger objectives. 
In this case, there is potentially a lot at stake between Trump and Xi. 
Their third face-to-face encounter since the start of Trump's second term, this summit is happening amid growing fears of an AI-led apocalypse as both countries race for dominance in the quickly growing industry. 
It's also taking place in the wake of a bitter US-China trade war that has only been resolved by a temporary truce, extended on this trip. 
The present exchange helps smooth over the differences and should be seen in the same way as the military flyovers, the pageantry and the state dinner, Kritenbrink says. 
"It's protocol and it's optics and it's gift giving all as a means to an end, which is stable US-China relations. 
"I'll take a fragile truce over a white-hot trade war any day of the week."

articles.title: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
articles.summary: China's economy and tech have developed at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing country By Fan Wang 
- Published 26 September 2026 
"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol". 
Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation. 
And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it. 
China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up. 
"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home. 
"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me." 
She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting". 
Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media. 
Image caption, 
About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently 
In Singapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. 
It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better. 
These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times". 
"Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore. 
"But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it." 
He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia. 
Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it. 
China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says 
Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air. 
"The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected. 
This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. 
One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful." 
Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us." 
Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things." 
Image caption, 
Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures 
Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation. 
Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money." 
And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says. 
Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them. 
They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job. 
Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects 
Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward. 
Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition. 
The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home. 
"When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution." 
About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles". 
Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation. 
But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity. 
"If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

articles.title: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry
articles.summary: Australia is increasingly concerned about China's military might - but Beijing is also its biggest trade partner.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 2024. Relations between the two countries have been rocky in recent years By Katy Watson Australia correspondent ,  Reporting from Townsville, North Queensland 
- Published 6 hours ago 
Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead. 
Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might. 
" We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan. 
"Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important." 
War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation. 
With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific , there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower. 
But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner . 
Image source, BBC: Katy Watson Image caption, 
Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan says Australia is rehearsing for "the worst type of war" 
It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight. 
"We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is. 
Binding tighter to the US 
The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific. 
"We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says. 
And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500. 
A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing. 
"Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said. 
"China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects." 
The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers. 
But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties. 
The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer. 
Image source, BBC: Katy Watson Image caption, 
The Southern Jackaroo exercises are aimed at improving defence cooperation in the Indo-Pacific 
But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US. 
"Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll. 
"Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States." 
The 'frenemy' 
While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China. 
Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner. 
Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer. 
Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015. 
The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs. 
And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up. 
A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years. 
Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges. 
In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China is Australia's biggest export market 
Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary. 
"There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments,"  says Lyons-Jones. 
This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US. 
Rise and fall of superpowers 
Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be". 
Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing. 
"The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says. 
Image source, PMO Australia Image caption, 
US President Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese. Australians have cooled on their relationship with the US under Trump 
But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump , the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one. 
"This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang. 
And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act. 
"There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says. 
"It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

articles.title: Seoul summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: Last week Zelensky revealed Ukraine had sent two captured North Koreans to South Korea - which Seoul says was meant to be a secret.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters/EPA Image caption, 
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky made an announcement concerning the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war last week - which South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has called "greatly disappointing" By Jake Kwon Seoul correspondent 
- Published 28 September 2026 
South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador after President Volodymyr Zelensky last week announced his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. 
Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo lodged a formal complaint with Andrii Vieshkin and expressed "strong regret" that Zelensky had revealed the transfer, which Seoul says was supposed to be a secret. 
The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. 
President Lee Jae Myung called the disclosure "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. 
Ukraine's foreign ministry declined to comment when approached by the BBC. 
In early 2025, Ukraine said its forces had captured two North Korean soldiers as prisoners of war in Russia's Kursk Oblast . 
After more than a year of negotiations between Seoul and Kyiv, Zelensky announced they had been transferred to South Korea at the UN General Assembly last Wednesday - adding they had not been "easy to capture alive". 
Seoul confirmed the news but sharply criticised Zelensky for allegedly breaking an agreement to keep the transfer a secret. 
This was partly to protect the North Koreans' families, President Lee's office said in a statement, which added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. 
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. 
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. 
Seoul demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. 
Lee faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure. The South Korean opposition accused him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. 
Lee, whose party takes a conciliatory approach to the North, has been making efforts to reopen peace talks, with little success. 
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. 
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. 
"When North Korea actively participates in a war in Europe, South Korea cannot remain a distant observer," said Mykhailo Podolyak, a senior adviser to Zelensky. 
"The transfer of defence technologies and capabilities from Seoul to Kyiv is not just about helping Ukraine; it is about South Korea protecting its own long-term security interests by containing the expansion of an aggressive totalitarian axis." 
This July, Seoul announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. 
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. 
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. 
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: Four bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan climbing group
articles.summary: Rescuers are still looking for 12 Nepalese cook staff who were preparing for climbers to ascend the Himlung Himal peak.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The avalanche struck Himlung Himal, a mountain popular with overseas climbers By Sean Seddon 
- Published 27 September 2026 Updated 9 hours ago 
Rescuers have recovered four bodies from the site of an avalanche that struck a climbing group camping in the Nepalese part of the Himalayas. 
A dozen people are still thought to be missing after a sheet of snow fell on the base camp of Himlung Himal peak on Manang district on Sunday morning. 
The group of Nepalese nationals, including climbers and support staff, had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp and fix ropes. 
Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet. 
Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams initially unable to reach the site. 
Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP that at least eight members of his expedition team had been reported missing. 
A rescue team consisting of experienced mountaineers was rushed from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, via helicopter. 
On Sunday, the first two bodies were found, with another two bodies discovered on Monday, the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, which sent out a rescue team, said in a social media post. 
The group said the team ascended the mountain hoping to find survivors. 
"Unfortunately, after extensive search efforts under extremely difficult conditions, four bodies were recovered, while 12 cook staff remain missing at Himlung Base Camp." 
"The avalanche was exceptionally large, with approximately 14 feet of snow covering the Base Camp area. Searching every section manually was extremely difficult and dangerous due to the depth of snow, freezing temperatures, and unstable conditions." 
The group said it had temporarily paused operations due to the conditions, but will continue to monitor and "make every possible effort to recover the remaining bodies when it becomes safe to do so". 
The Nepalese team caught in the avalanche had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain. 
Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry. 
Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches. 
The latest death of Nepalese climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan , including renowned British-Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja. 
It also comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August. 
More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements. 
Dangerous weather events have also affected other parts of Asia in the past week. 
Extreme weather in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has also killed more than 50 people, officials there said. 
Meanwhile, a flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok , Thailand because of heavy rainfall since Thursday, with people being urged to stay at home or move to higher floors. 
Earlier this week, a deadly typhoon that battered Tokyo, triggering landslides in neighbouring prefectures that killed four people. 
Typhoon Dujuan was the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", an area of warmer sea water that facilitates the formation of powerful storms.

articles.title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back
articles.summary: Big Bang played London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, marking a long-awaited return for the group that helped build the blueprint for modern K-pop.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Timothy Norris/Getty Images Image caption, 
Taeyang, G-Dragon and Daesung of BigBang perform during the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival By Jiji Ahn 
- Published 27 September 2026 
A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean. 
An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back. 
Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour. 
Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert - they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history. 
As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming. 
Image caption, 
Inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium 
For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia. 
Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia. 
The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal. 
Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking. 
Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio, comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community. 
By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging. 
The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful. 
Image source, YG Entertainment Image caption, 
G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung on stage with dancers 
In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards. 
When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours. 
They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible. 
Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List. 
"When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool. 
"Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds. 
"Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be." 
Image source, YG Entertainment Image caption, 
G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung celebrating their 20th anniversary during the XX: Cosmos World Tour 
Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies. 
But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre. 
For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live. 
"They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore. 
"They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me." 
The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS. 
Image caption, 
Fans arrived kitted out with Big Bang merchandise 
And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong. 
In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks. 
But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise. 
"Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology." 
The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow. 
Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years. 
Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, co-ordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances. 
Image caption, 
Fans exchanging handmade gifts outside the stadium 
Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success. 
South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus. 
Then came the scandals. 
In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group. 
Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal. 
It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars. 
South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement. 
Image caption, 
Fans with their merchandise, holding up free banners ahead of the show 
Although the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience. 
Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more. 
"Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs." 
The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong. 
Image caption, 
Fans meeting up ahead of the concert 
The K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition. 
Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted. 
While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances. 
Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets. 
"I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy." 
For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance. 
"I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin. 
"Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream." 
Image caption, 
Nicole and her son Arthur attended the concert to celebrate his 8th birthday 
Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube. 
"Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um. 
"It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations." 
While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life. 
As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd. 
Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut. 
As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop.

articles.title: Remains of dozens of suspected kidnap victims found in Nigerian forests
articles.summary: Investigations are ongoing to establish the identities of at least 28 people whose remains were recovered by police.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Abia State Police Command Image caption, 
Human skulls and bones were found by police in the Umuaku and Nneato forests By Chris Ewokor ,  BBC Africa ,  Reporting from Abuja   and   Olivia Ireland 
- Published 9 hours ago 
The skulls and bones of at least 28 people have been recovered from suspected criminal camps in Nigerian forests. 
Police in the south-eastern state of Abia are investigating the identities of the remains found in the Umuaku and Nneato forests on Saturday after a security operation was carried out in the Umunneochi area. 
Police spokeswoman Maureen Chinaka said the suspects fled when police arrived. 
The discovery is likely to revive concerns about kidnapping gangs operating in remote forests across parts of south-eastern Nigeria, where criminal groups have frequently targeted motorists, travellers and residents for ransom. 
According to Abia State Police Command, the raids were launched following intelligence reports about suspected criminal activity in the forests. 
Officers suspect the remains belong to kidnapping victims, although forensic and other investigations are ongoing to establish their identities and the circumstances surrounding their deaths. 
"Upon arrival of the Command's tactical operatives at the camps, the suspects fled. The criminal camps were subsequently dismantled. A total of twenty-eight human skulls and bones, suspected to be kidnap victims, were recovered," Chinaka said in a statement. 
Police said surveillance had been intensified in the area as officers sought to track down those who fled. 
Abia state police commissioner Wilfred Afolabi said the operation was part of an ongoing campaign to dismantle criminal hideouts in the state. 
Police have appealed to residents to report suspicious activity and security concerns as efforts continue to identify the victims and determine whether the remains are connected to unresolved kidnapping cases in the region. 
Authorities have previously discovered decomposing bodies believed to be linked to kidnapping activities during security raids in Umunneochi . 
Separately over the weekend, more than 80 people, mostly women, were seized in separate mass kidnappings in two states in the country's north. 
In an attack on Sunday, nearly 50 farmers were abducted by gunmen in Niger State. 
On Sunday, about 40 other women were kidnapped in the neighbouring state of Zamfara, according to two security reports seen by AFP and a local source. 
Abductions for ransom have become a key source of income for criminals, including bandits and militant Islamists, in northern Nigeria.

Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island 
Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday. 
David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.” 
On Monday, Chinese state media praised the “extraordinary level of courtesy” that Trump had shown Xi on the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington . 
The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn (£10.5bn), after a record multibillion-dollar deal was announced in December last year. 
View image in fullscreen 
Donald Trump and his wife, Melania, hosting Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the White House last week. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 
Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned . At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China. ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes 
Read more 
Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself. 
Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take it. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence”, according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. 
After Perdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times the US had no plans to sell arms to China , while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.” 
China is a net exporter of weapons. Of the arms that it does import, most come from Russia, but the volume is rapidly falling thanks to advances in China’s own military manufacturing capacity. China’s arms imports fell by 72% between 2021 and 2025 compared with the previous five years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. 
Before the interview, the Taiwanese deputy foreign minister, Chen Ming-chi, spoke of the severe military threat China posed. 
“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei. 
View image in fullscreen 
Taiwanese honour guards during a flag-lowering ceremony at Liberty Square in Taipei, on the eve of Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington last week, during which he urged Trump to oppose ‘Taiwan independence’. Photograph: Daniel Ceng/Anadolu/Getty Images 
On Sunday, a Taiwanese official, Shen Yu-chung, also pushed back on what he said was an attempt by Beijing to “falsely claim that the Chinese Communist party and the US were allies” in the second world war. A fact sheet released by the White House after the Trump-Xi summit had said China and the US “fought side by side to win” in the war. 
China’s government during the second world war was the Republic of China led by Chiang Kai-shek. Chiang’s government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, who established the People’s Republic of China in 1949. 
In recent years Taiwan has sought to emphasise its history of fighting alongside western democratic allies as it hopes to bolster international support against aggression from Beijing. 
Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan. 
Perdue told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.
